destination.title: Your School Can Search You Without a Warrant — the Supreme Court Said So

short48: A fourteen-year-old is caught smoking in a school bathroom.
Minutes later a vice principal is emptying
her purse across his desk.
Does the Fourth Amendment even follow you into school?
She says she doesn't smoke.
He opens the bag anyway.
On top a pack of cigarettes.
Beside them rolling papers.
He keeps searching and finds marijuana and
letters that read like she was dealing.
Her lawyers said the search was illegal.
Throw it all out.
The school said the Constitution stops at the door.
The other side said make him get
a warrant like a cop.
In nineteen eighty-five the Supreme Court refused both.
The Fourth Amendment does follow you into school.
But here's the catch.
Inside a school the bar is lower. No warrant.
No probable cause.
Just reasonable suspicion kept in proportion.
Six to three that's the rule for
every backpack since.
Watch the full case on the channel.
Follow for more.

candidate_payload_lines: You have been taught, in a loose sort of way, that the government cannot just search your things without a good reason, and usually not without a warrant.
Because she is a minor, the court records never print her full name.
Everything inside it, they argue, is the fruit of an illegal search, a violation of her Fourth Amendment rights, and none of it should be allowed as evidence against her.
Probable cause, they argued, had guarded ordinary people for two centuries without paralyzing anyone, and no one had shown a school could not live within it.
But the bar they have to clear is lower than a police officer's, and that is the part almost nobody knows until the bag is already open.
If you walked in here assuming students either hold the full Fourth Amendment or none of it, and you can now see it is a third thing sitting in between, that is worth a like.
era_note: 1980s New Jersey public high school. The search happened in 1980 and the ruling came down in 1985, so every generated plate reads early-1980s American school interior. Stock footage must stay era-neutral - lockers, corridors, doors, hands, benches - with no smartphones, no flat screens and no dated signage in frame.

shorts.angle: The two-part test means a lawful school search can become an unlawful one halfway through, because the second prong measures how far the search went, not why it began.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: How far did the search of that one purse actually go before anyone asked whether it was still lawful?
shorts.loop_join: L8 says legality is decided by where a search stops, which is the exact claim L1 opens with when it says a search can start legal and turn illegal partway through.

lines.text: A school search can start out legal and turn illegal partway through. The Supreme Court built a limit into how far it may go.
source_lines: That second prong is not decoration. It means a search can outgrow its own excuse.

lines.text: In nineteen eighty-five, in a case about a fourteen-year-old's purse, the Court wrote a two-part test that still governs school bags.
source_lines: It built a two-part test, and that test is the real inheritance of this case.
It still governs your bag today.

lines.text: The first part asks whether there was a real reason to begin: grounds to suspect a student broke a law or rule.
source_lines: First, the search has to be justified at its inception.

In the Court's own words, there must be reasonable grounds for suspecting that the search will turn up evidence that the student has violated or is violating either the law or the rules of the school.

lines.text: The second part asks how far it went. A search must stay reasonably related in scope to whatever justified it.
source_lines: Second, the search has to be reasonably related in scope to the circumstances that justified it in the first place.

lines.text: It cannot be excessively intrusive in light of the student's age and sex, and the nature of whatever rule was supposedly broken.
source_lines: The measures the official uses must be reasonably related to the objectives of the search, and not excessively intrusive in light of the age and sex of the student and the nature of the infraction.

lines.text: A rumor about one cigarette cannot be ridden into something far more invasive. Stretch the search past what set it off and it fails.
source_lines: If the reason you were pulled aside was a rumor about a single cigarette, an official cannot ride that into something far more invasive.
Stretch the search past what set it off, and it fails the test even when the first prong was cleanly satisfied.

lines.text: The Court said both parts were met there. The report of smoking justified opening the bag, and each step followed what the last revealed.
source_lines: Applied to the purse, the majority said the search cleared both prongs.
Each step was tied to what the step before it had already revealed.

lines.text: So the legality of a school search is not settled when it begins. It is decided by where it stops.
source_lines: A search needs a real, specific reason at the start.
And it has to stay in proportion as it goes, so that a report of something small cannot be used to justify taking a student completely apart.

shorts.avoids: Short 48 told the story of the bathroom, the emptied purse and the 6-3 holding; this cut is only the scope prong, the half of the test that limits how far an official may keep going.

shorts.angle: The lowered school standard was written for educators alone, and the Court kept a higher standard in reserve for the moment a police officer runs or directs the search.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: What did the Court say a school official may do on his own authority, and where exactly does that authority stop?
shorts.loop_join: L8 says the same bag opened by a principal or by an officer is two different questions, which sends the viewer straight back into L1's statement that the lower standard was never written for police.

lines.text: The lower standard that lets a school search your bag was never written for police. When an officer runs it, a higher one returns.
source_lines: This case is about school officials acting on their own.
When the police get involved, when an officer runs the search or directs it from behind, a different and higher standard can come back into the picture.

lines.text: The Court said so plainly. The lowered bar was built for educators keeping order in a school, not for law enforcement.
source_lines: The lowered bar was built for educators keeping order in a school.

lines.text: Not for law enforcement using a school as a shortcut around the warrant an officer would otherwise need to get.
source_lines: It was not built for law enforcement using that school as a shortcut around the warrant it would otherwise need.

lines.text: Three justices refused to sign the lowered bar at all. Brennan, Marshall and Stevens broke with the majority over that exact trade.
source_lines: Three justices would not sign all of that.
In opinions concurring in part and dissenting in part, Justices Brennan, Marshall, and Stevens broke with the majority.

lines.text: Their worry was the standard itself. Trade probable cause for reasonable suspicion, they warned, and you hand officials a power easy to misuse.
source_lines: Their worry was the lowered bar itself.
Trade probable cause for something as soft as reasonable suspicion, they warned, and you hand school officials a broad power that is easy to misuse, with a young person's privacy as the price.

lines.text: Probable cause had guarded ordinary people for two centuries, they argued, and nobody had shown a school could not live within it.
source_lines: Probable cause, they argued, had guarded ordinary people for two centuries without paralyzing anyone, and no one had shown a school could not live within it.

lines.text: Water the standard down to a hunch, they cautioned, and the students searched on the thinnest reasons have the least power to push back.
source_lines: Water the standard down to a hunch, they cautioned, and the students searched on the thinnest reasons are the ones with the least power to push back.

lines.text: So the answer depends on who is standing there. The same bag, opened by a principal or by an officer, is two different questions.
source_lines: This case is about school officials acting on their own.
The lowered bar was built for educators keeping order in a school.
